paper.title_en: Long-Term Evolution of Hills-Captured Stars with TDE Disk Collisions: Links to Repeating Nuclear Transients
paper.abstract_en: Quasi-periodic eruptions (QPEs) and repeating partial tidal disruption event (rpTDE) candidates are widely interpreted as being powered by a star on an hours-to-years orbit around a massive black hole (MBH). Every such orbiter model presupposes a star delivered onto an extraordinarily compact orbit without being destroyed, but it is unclear whether this is achievable. We follow the coupled orbital and stellar evolution of stars captured by the Hills mechanism, combining gas drag and per-collision mass loss from recurrent TDE disks with gravitational-wave (GW) orbital decay and stochastic two-body relaxation in a Monte Carlo model. Conventionally, the EMRI-formation criterion is based on comparing the timescales of GW decay and orbital angular momentum relaxation. We find that this criterion severely overestimates the EMRI rate: for relaxation timescales shorter than a Hubble time, most Hills-captured stars are tidally disrupted before GW emission can circularize the stellar orbit. Instead, TDE-disk drag plays a crucial role in the orbital evolution and can boost the fraction of stars reaching QPE orbits by an order of magnitude or more, assuming that the disk aspect ratio is relatively large $H/r \sim 0.1$. We also find that collisional ablation imposes a minimum orbital period that rises with MBH mass and precludes sub-day orbits for $M_{\rm BH} \gtrsim 10^6\,M_\odot$, unless GWs alone can drive orbital decay faster than orbital relaxation. This can explain the observed preference of short-period QPEs for low-mass MBHs. Most known rpTDEs lie below the Hills-capture period minimum and thus require additional orbital decay, which TDE-disk drag can plausibly supply. These results support the viability of the orbiter model; our predictions of the MBH mass and orbital period distributions can be used to further test this model.
